opus-5.5.text:
Well, so the problem with joint embedding architectures is that if you just train them to make the representation of two views of the same thing similar, the system can cheat: it can simply ignore the input and produce a constant output. That's the collapse. So you need some way of preventing it.

Contrastive methods were historically the first approach. Actually, I worked on this in the early nineties with Siamese networks for signature verification, and later with Raia Hadsell and Sumit Chopra around 2005-2006. The idea is that you push together representations of things that are compatible, and you push apart representations of things that are not. It works. Things like SimCLR and MoCo showed it can work quite well. But I've become fairly negative about contrastive methods in the long run, for a simple reason: in high-dimensional representation spaces, the number of ways two things can be different is enormous. To shape the energy landscape properly you need to sample a huge number of negatives, and the efficiency scales badly with dimension. So you end up with representations that are relatively low-dimensional, or you need giant batches. It's not the way forward, in my opinion.

Then there are the distillation-type methods: BYOL, SimSiam, DINO, and in a sense our own I-JEPA and V-JEPA use a version of this. You have a student network and a teacher network whose weights are an exponential moving average of the student's, with a predictor on one side and a stop-gradient. Empirically, these work remarkably well; they don't collapse, and they give very good features. The problem is that we don't completely understand why they work. There's some theory now, but it's a bit like a trick that happens to not collapse rather than something that is guaranteed by the objective. That makes me a little uncomfortable.

What I prefer, at least conceptually, are the regularized methods, the information-maximization approaches, like Barlow Twins and VICReg, which we developed at FAIR. There, instead of negatives, you have an explicit term that keeps the variance of each component of the representation above a threshold and decorrelates the components from each other. So you're essentially maximizing the information content of the representation, in a crude way, while minimizing prediction error. This is non-contrastive, it scales better with dimension, and you understand what's going on.

So to summarize: contrastive, I think, is a dead end in the long term because of the curse of dimensionality. Distillation works very well in practice, and it's what a lot of the best systems use today, but it's a bit mysterious. And regularized, information-maximizing methods are where I think the principled answer lies, even though there's still work to do to make them as practical as the distillation ones. And the bigger point is that all of this is in service of something more important: learning world models with joint embedding predictive architectures, rather than generative models that try to predict every pixel.

r001.rationale: The response says contrastive methods require huge numbers of negatives in high-dimensional spaces and that their efficiency scales badly with dimension.

r002.rationale: The response says researchers do not completely understand why distillation methods work and describes their resistance to collapse as not guaranteed by the objective.

r003.rationale: The response says the reason distillation avoids collapse is not fully understood, but does not state that the training fails to minimize the cost function it appears to minimize.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first let me frame the problem, because the question of collapse is really the central question of the whole joint embedding approach.

In a joint embedding architecture you take two views, x and y, that are related in some way. Two crops of the same image, a video frame and the next frame, whatever. You run each through an encoder, and you train the system so that the two embeddings are predictable from one another, perhaps through a small predictor on one branch. The energy you are minimizing is basically the prediction error in representation space. The problem is that there is a trivial solution: the encoder outputs a constant, the prediction error is zero everywhere, and you have learned nothing. The representation has collapsed. So every method in this family is really a different answer to the question "how do you prevent that constant solution?"

Contrastive methods are the oldest answer, and I have to say I was partly responsible for them. We did this with Siamese networks in the early nineties for signature verification, and later with DrLIM in the mid-2000s. The idea is simple. You pull the embeddings of compatible pairs together, and you push the embeddings of incompatible pairs apart. So you need negative samples, points where you explicitly push the energy up. Modern versions like SimCLR, MoCo, and InfoNCE-style objectives are the same idea at scale.

My assessment is that contrastive methods work, but they are fundamentally inefficient, and I think they are a dead end in the long run. The reason is dimensional. If your representation space is high-dimensional, say a few hundred or a few thousand dimensions, the number of negative samples you need to shape the energy landscape properly grows very quickly. You are trying to push the energy up everywhere outside the data manifold, one point at a time, in a space that is mostly empty. You can never sample enough negatives. People compensate with enormous batch sizes, memory banks, hard negative mining, and they get decent results, but it is a brute force fight against the curse of dimensionality. The second problem is that the choice of negatives is a kind of hidden supervision. You are telling the system what counts as different, and if two images in the batch are actually semantically similar, you are forcing them apart for no good reason.

Distillation methods are more interesting to me, and they are what I would call non-contrastive. BYOL, SimSiam, DINO, and then our own work with I-JEPA and V-JEPA are in this family. You have a student encoder and a teacher encoder, the teacher is typically an exponential moving average of the student, and there is a stop-gradient on the teacher branch. The student has to predict the teacher's representation. There are no negatives at all.

Now, the honest truth is that for a while nobody fully understood why this does not collapse. Empirically it does not, but the stop-gradient plus the EMA plus the predictor create a dynamic that is somewhat mysterious. There has been good theoretical work since then, showing that the predictor and the asymmetry act to prevent the degenerate solution and that the system ends up learning something like the eigenstructure of the data. But I would not say it is a clean story. It is a bit of alchemy that happens to work very well. The upside is that it scales beautifully. The cost per sample does not depend on how many negatives you can afford. And in I-JEPA and V-JEPA we showed that if you do the prediction in representation space rather than pixel space, you learn abstract features, you can ignore unpredictable details, and the downstream performance is excellent.

There is also a third category that I think is cleaner conceptually, which is the regularized methods, things like Barlow Twins and VICReg from my group. There you prevent collapse explicitly, by maximizing the information content of the embedding. You maintain the variance of each dimension above a threshold and you decorrelate the dimensions. The energy is not pushed up at sampled negative points, it is pushed up through a regularizer that says the volume of the representation space that gets low energy must be limited. I like this because the collapse prevention is a stated objective rather than an emergent property of a training trick. In practice, though, distillation currently gives somewhat better results at scale, and I think the field has mostly gravitated toward it for that reason.

So if you ask me to rank them: contrastive, I would say we should move away from. It works, but it does not scale in the way we need and it fights the geometry of the space. Distillation is the current workhorse, highly effective, somewhat under-theorized. And regularized, information-maximization approaches are where I would like the theory to go, because they make explicit what the distillation methods are doing implicitly. The ultimate goal is a system that learns a world model by predicting in abstract representation space, and whichever anti-collapse mechanism we use has to be the one that lets us do that at the scale of video, with hierarchical, multi-step prediction. That is where I think the real action is in the next few years.

r001.rationale: It says the number of negatives needed grows quickly in high-dimensional representation spaces and that contrastive methods cannot sample enough negatives, calling this a fight against the curse of dimensionality.

r002.rationale: It says the reason distillation avoids collapse was not fully understood, describes the explanation as mysterious and the theory as not clean, despite later theoretical work.

r003.rationale: It describes the prediction error as the cost being minimized, but does not state that distillation training fails to minimize that apparent cost.

astra-6.text:
They’re two ways of dealing with the central difficulty of joint embedding architectures. You take two views of an image, run them through two networks, and train the representations to agree. But if that’s your entire objective, there’s a trivial solution: the networks output the same constant for every image. They agree perfectly, but they haven’t learned anything useful.

Contrastive learning prevents this by also pushing apart the representations of different images. It works very well, but I’m not convinced that explicitly pushing examples apart is necessary. You have to choose negative examples, and two images that you treat as negatives may actually have very similar semantic content. There’s also a computational cost to comparing lots of examples.

With distillation approaches, you have a student predicting the representation produced by a teacher. Often the teacher is a moving average of the student, and you stop gradients through the teacher. These methods can work remarkably well without explicit negatives. But distillation by itself doesn’t guarantee that you avoid collapse. The asymmetry, the normalization, the way you update the teacher—all those details matter.

My preference is to make the anti-collapse mechanism explicit. You can encourage the representations of two views to agree, while also requiring that each component have sufficient variance across examples and reducing redundancy between components. That’s the idea behind VICReg. You don’t need to push particular pairs of images apart; you need to make sure the representation retains information. So I see contrastive learning as an effective approach, but not a necessary ingredient of joint embedding architectures.

r002.rationale: It says distillation does not guarantee avoiding collapse and that implementation details matter, but does not discuss a lack of satisfactory theoretical explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
The problem is that if you train two branches of a joint embedding architecture simply to produce the same representation for related inputs, there is a trivial solution: they can produce the same constant for everything. The loss is perfectly happy, but the representation is useless.

Contrastive learning prevents this by also pushing apart the representations of inputs that are supposed to be different. It works very well, but I don’t think it’s the most satisfactory solution. You have to choose negative examples, and two examples that you treat as negatives may actually share precisely the semantic properties you want the system to learn. You also spend a lot of computation comparing examples.

Distillation approaches are interesting because they show that explicit negatives aren’t necessary. You train a student to predict the representation produced by a teacher, often a moving average of the student. But distillation by itself doesn’t exclude the constant solution. The asymmetry, normalization, centering, or other constraints are doing important work in preventing collapse.

My preference is to make those constraints explicit. With a method like VICReg, you encourage representations of related inputs to agree, keep sufficient variance in each component across examples, and reduce redundancy between components. So you have an invariance term and terms that prevent collapse, without having to push individual examples away from one another. That’s a cleaner way of formulating the problem, in my view.
